name: Nephrology & AKI
sub: KDIGO staging, RRT, CRRT, nephrotoxins, hepatorenal, rhabdomyolysis

cards.q: State the KDIGO definition of acute kidney injury.
cards.a: Any of: serum creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours; creatinine ≥1.5 × baseline within 7 days; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.
cards.src: KDIGO 2012 (KDIGO 2026 AKI/AKD update is in draft; adds cystatin C and biomarker criteria)

cards.q: State the KDIGO AKI stages.
cards.a: Stage 1: creatinine 1.5–1.9× baseline or ≥0.3 mg/dL rise; UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h. Stage 2: 2.0–2.9×; UO <0.5 for ≥12 h. Stage 3: ≥3.0×, creatinine ≥4.0 mg/dL or RRT; UO <0.3 for ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h.

cards.q: How do you separate pre-renal azotaemia from ATN?
cards.a: Pre-renal: FENa <1% (FEUrea <35% if on diuretics), urine osmolality >500 mOsm/kg, bland sediment, quick response to volume. ATN: FENa >2%, isosthenuria, muddy brown granular casts.

cards.q: List the classic indications for urgent renal replacement therapy.
cards.a: Refractory hyperkalaemia, refractory metabolic acidosis, refractory fluid overload, uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding) and dialysable intoxications (e.g. lithium, methanol, salicylate, ethylene glycol).

cards.q: What did STARRT-AKI and AKIKI-2 show about timing of RRT?
cards.a: An accelerated strategy did not improve 90-day survival and increased RRT dependence and adverse events; a watchful-waiting approach with RRT only for urgent indications is reasonable.

cards.q: What effluent dose is recommended for CRRT?
cards.a: A delivered dose of 20–25 mL/kg/h (prescribe about 25–30 mL/kg/h to allow for downtime).

cards.q: Differentiate CVVH, CVVHD and CVVHDF.
cards.a: CVVH uses convection (ultrafiltration with replacement fluid); CVVHD uses diffusion with dialysate; CVVHDF combines both for solute clearance across molecular sizes.

cards.q: What is the preferred anticoagulation for CRRT and what is citrate toxicity?
cards.a: Regional citrate anticoagulation for patients without contraindications (liver failure, shock with high lactate). Toxicity: total-to-ionised calcium ratio >2.5, high anion gap acidosis, falling ionised calcium and rising total calcium.

cards.q: How long is a SLED/PIRRT session?
cards.a: About 6–12 hours of reduced-intensity, extended dialysis, combining haemodynamic tolerance close to CRRT with the logistics of intermittent therapy.

cards.q: List common nephrotoxins in the ICU.
cards.a: Aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, vancomycin (especially with piperacillin-tazobactam), NSAIDs, contrast, ACE inhibitors/ARBs in volume depletion, colistin, hydroxyethyl starch.

cards.q: How is contrast-associated AKI prevented?
cards.a: Identify risk, use the smallest possible dose of low- or iso-osmolar contrast, ensure euvolaemia (isotonic IV fluids), and avoid concurrent nephrotoxins. N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate offer no clear advantage.

cards.q: How should rhabdomyolysis be managed?
cards.a: Early aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation (aim for urine output 200–300 mL/h in severe cases), treat hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia only if symptomatic, stop offending drugs, and consider RRT for refractory complications.

cards.q: What is the treatment of hepatorenal syndrome–AKI?
cards.a: Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins, albumin 1 g/kg (max 100 g) for 2 days, then terlipressin (or noradrenaline infusion) with albumin; consider TIPS or liver transplant.

cards.q: Which urine findings suggest glomerulonephritis versus interstitial nephritis?
cards.a: Red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells suggest glomerulonephritis; white cell casts and eosinophils suggest acute interstitial nephritis.

cards.q: What is abdominal compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Sustained intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction. Measure bladder pressure; treat with sedation and analgesia, decompress the stomach and bowel, drain fluid and, if refractory, perform decompressive laparotomy.

cards.q: How do you perform a furosemide stress test?
cards.a: Give furosemide 1.0 mg/kg (1.5 mg/kg if previous exposure) and measure urine output over 2 hours; less than 200 mL suggests progression to stage 3 AKI.

cards.q: Why is hydroxyethyl starch avoided?
cards.a: It increases the risks of AKI, renal replacement and mortality in sepsis and critical illness.

cards.q: What is the typical vascular access for acute dialysis?
cards.a: A non-tunnelled dialysis catheter in the right internal jugular vein (12–15 Fr), with femoral veins as an alternative and left jugular as a third option.

cards.q: A patient with oliguric AKI has K⁺ 7.2 mmol/L and peaked T waves. What is the first drug to give?
o: IV calcium gluconate 10% (10–30 mL) to stabilise the myocardium
cards.e: Give calcium first for ECG changes, then insulin with dextrose and salbutamol to shift potassium; remove it with RRT if anuric.

cards.q: Which of these meets KDIGO stage 3 AKI?
cards.e: Stage 3 includes creatinine ≥4.0 mg/dL or ≥3× baseline. A rise to 1.6 is stage 1; 2.4 is stage 2; low UO for 8 hours is stage 1.

cards.q: What is expected from the KDIGO 2026 AKI/AKD guideline?
cards.a: The first major update since 2012 (public-review draft, comments closed May 2026; check for the final version). It adds acute kidney disease (AKD) to the framework, updated definitions using functional criteria and structural biomarkers, a suggestion to use cystatin C when creatinine is less accurate (2B), and updated guidance on kidney replacement therapy timing, modality, dosing and discontinuation, plus follow-up care after AKI.
